The same fund at death in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF, or a taxable account: what heirs actually receive

A balanced fund held for decades is taxed by the account it sits in, and the biggest tax bill often comes on the final return. Follow one fund in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF and a taxable account to the year of death: the deemed disposition, the full RRIF inclusion, probate, the spouse rollover and the yearly tax along the way.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The same fund at death in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF, and a taxable account: what heirs receive

Interactive planning lab

TFSA: received by a child or other heir after 15 years$415,785.64
RRSP or RRIF: received by a child or other heir$228,682.1
Taxable account: received by a child or other heir$334,882.84
Income tax due on the final return, all three accounts$226,012.55
Income tax deferred to the spouse by the rollover$0
Probate or estate fee, all three accounts$5,692.26
Tax paid on taxable-account distributions while alive$26,268.76
Taxable account: unrealized gain at death$172,928.96

Starting from $200,000 of the same fund in each account and 5% a year, the TFSA and the RRSP or RRIF both reach $415,786 after 15 years; the taxable account reaches $379,484 after $26,269 of tax on distributions along the way. At a 45% rate, the RRSP or RRIF loses $187,104 to the final return and the taxable account $38,909 on half of its $172,929 gain. With beneficiaries named on the registered accounts, only the taxable account passes through the estate, at a 1.5% fee. A child or other heir receives $415,786, $228,682 and $334,883. The RRSP or RRIF figure is lower partly because its contributions were deducted when made: its balance was never after-tax money. Rates and rules are simplified; this is not tax or estate advice.

The central idea

In the default case, CAD 200,000 of the same fund in each account, growing 5% a year for 15 years, is worth CAD 415,786 in the TFSA and the RRSP or RRIF. A child receives all of the TFSA, but only CAD 228,682 of the RRIF after a 45% final-return rate on its whole value, and CAD 334,883 of the taxable account after CAD 26,269 of tax on distributions while alive, CAD 38,909 on half of a CAD 172,929 gain at death and a 1.5% probate fee. A spouse can defer almost all of that tax, but it is postponed, not removed. The RRIF gap is mostly the tax deduction it gave when contributions were made, so the accounts are not ranked by this alone.

01

The fund is the same; the account decides the tax

A balanced fund does not carry its own tax treatment. The same units can sit in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF, or an ordinary taxable account, and each account applies different rules to the same growth: while you are alive, when you withdraw, and at death. The final return is often where the largest single bill appears, because the Income Tax Act treats death as a sale of everything at once.

This guide follows one fund, with the same return, through all three accounts to the year of death and asks what an heir actually receives. It is built for long-term investors who expect to keep part of their savings for life, and it separates three costs that are often blurred: tax paid each year in a taxable account, income tax on the final return, and probate or estate administration fees.

02

Three accounts, three rules at death

  • Taxable account. Section 70(5) deems the person to have disposed of each capital property immediately before death at fair market value. CRA’s guide says this includes investments like mutual funds. The gain above the adjusted cost base is a capital gain, and half of it is taxable on the final return at the person’s rates.
  • RRSP or RRIF. Section 146.3(6) deems the last annuitant of a RRIF to have received the fund’s fair market value immediately before death, and CRA says to include that amount in the deceased’s income. All of it is income, not half: contributions were deducted and growth was never taxed.
  • TFSA. CRA says a designated beneficiary does not pay tax on amounts received up to the TFSA’s fair market value on the date of death; earnings after death and before the account is settled are taxable.

The model applies one rate you enter to all income added to the final return. Large RRIF balances push income through several brackets, so the rate is closer to an average over the added amount than to a single bracket rate.

03

The default case: CAD 200,000 each, 15 years at 5%

The first chart splits each account’s value at death. The TFSA and the RRSP or RRIF both grow to CAD 415,786. A child receives the whole TFSA, because the beneficiary is named on the account and no tax is due. From the RRIF, CAD 187,104 goes to the final return at 45% and CAD 228,682 reaches the child.

The taxable account starts with a cost base of 70% of its value and pays out 2% a year as distributions, which are reinvested and taxed at 30% each year; the tax is paid by redeeming units. That costs CAD 26,269 over the 15 years and leaves CAD 379,484. At death the unrealized gain is CAD 172,929; half of it taxed at 45% is CAD 38,909. Held in one name, the account also passes through the estate, and a 1.5% fee takes CAD 5,692, leaving CAD 334,883. The reinvested distributions guide shows the yearly part in detail.

04

Why the RRIF number is not a verdict on the RRSP

Comparing CAD 200,000 in an RRSP with CAD 200,000 in a TFSA is not like for like. The RRSP balance was built from deducted contributions, so part of it always belonged to the tax system. At a 45% rate, CAD 200,000 in an RRSP is roughly equivalent to CAD 110,000 in a TFSA. Grow both at 5% for 15 years and the TFSA is worth CAD 228,682, exactly what the child receives from the RRIF. When the rate at contribution and the rate at death are the same, the two accounts end level.

The account matters when those rates differ. A deduction taken at 30% and a final return taxed at 45% costs the estate; a deduction at 45% and modest RRIF withdrawals taxed at 30% during retirement can do the opposite. The RRSP and TFSA tax timing guide covers that choice for money saved from pay; this guide is about money already in each account.

05

The longer the wait, the wider the gaps

The second chart repeats the calculation for every year of death from today to 40 years out, for a child or other heir. The TFSA and RRIF lines grow at the same rate with a fixed proportional gap. The taxable line falls further behind the TFSA over time, because tax on distributions is paid every year and the deferred gain keeps growing until death taxes half of it.

The heatmap puts that in proportion. With the default settings, the taxable account delivers about 88% of the TFSA after 5 years, 84% after 10, 77% after 20 and 72% after 30. Higher returns widen the gap. A fund that distributes mostly interest is taxed more heavily each year than one that distributes little, as the income-type guide shows, and room limits mean many long-term investors hold some money in each account.

06

A spouse can postpone the tax, not erase it

The third chart compares a child with a spouse or common-law partner. CRA says capital property transferred to a surviving spouse can roll over at its cost, postponing the gain until the spouse sells or is deemed to sell it, and that RRIF property paid to a surviving spouse and transferred to their own plan can be reported and deducted by the spouse. A TFSA can pass to a spouse named as successor holder. In the default case the spouse receives CAD 415,786 from each registered account and CAD 373,792 from the taxable account, with CAD 226,013 of income tax deferred.

That deferred amount is still owed when the spouse withdraws from the RRIF, sells the fund or dies. It may be charged at a lower or higher rate depending on the spouse’s other income. Rollovers have conditions, including timing limits and how the beneficiary is named, and a financially dependent child or grandchild can also qualify for some RRSP and RRIF rollovers. These details are not modelled.

07

Probate is a separate cost, and naming a beneficiary can avoid it

Probate or estate administration fees are set by each province and apply to assets that pass through the estate under the will. Ontario’s estate administration tax, for example, is CAD 15 for every CAD 1,000 of estate value above CAD 50,000, with no tax on estates of CAD 50,000 or less. The model applies your flat rate to the taxable account, which is assumed to be held in one name, and to the registered accounts only when no beneficiary is named on them. Set the named-beneficiary switch to 0 and the probate fee in the default case rises from CAD 5,692 to CAD 18,166; the TFSA amount received falls to CAD 409,549.

Fees and their exemptions vary widely, and Quebec handles both wills and beneficiary designations differently; CRA notes that Quebec does not recognize successor-holder designations on most TFSAs. Joint ownership, trusts and insurance are other routes with their own tax and legal consequences.

08

What this means for a long-term fund plan

  • Choosing the account is part of choosing the investment. The same balanced fund can deliver very different amounts to heirs depending on where it is held.
  • A TFSA is the only one of the three in which growth reaches a beneficiary without income tax, but its room is limited; investors who expect to leave money often fill it first.
  • A large RRIF at death can be taxed at top rates. Planned withdrawals during life, at lower rates, can reduce that, at the cost of paying tax sooner; the RRIF minimum guide shows the required payments.
  • In a taxable account, a fund that realizes and distributes little keeps more growth deferred, but the gain is still taxed at death unless it rolls to a spouse or is donated in kind, as the in-kind donation guide explains.
  • The estate liquidity guide covers how long the estate may wait before it can pay those bills.

09

What the model leaves out

  • Returns, distribution rates and tax rates are constant. Real funds rise and fall, distributions change and tax rates depend on income in each year.
  • No RRIF minimum withdrawals are modelled; a real RRIF pays out every year after it is opened, and those amounts are taxed when paid.
  • Capital losses at death, the year-of-death treatment of other income, foreign tax, the alternative minimum tax and changes after death are not modelled; a loss is shown as no tax rather than a credit.
  • Probate is a flat rate on value at death, ignoring provincial thresholds and the deduction rules for debts.
  • None of this is tax, legal or estate advice. Rules have conditions and change; an estate plan needs a professional who knows the person’s province and family.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. All four charts are hypothetical calculations with constant returns and rates you set. The rules they apply come from the Income Tax Act (sections 70(5), 70(6) and 146.3(6), current to the date reviewed), CRA guidance on final returns and TFSA beneficiaries reviewed 27 October 2026, and Ontario’s estate administration tax as one example of a probate fee. No official statistics are used. Nothing here is tax, legal or estate advice. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 70 ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026. Subsection 70(5): deemed disposition of each capital property immediately before death at fair market value, and the heir’s cost equal to that value. Subsection 70(6): rollover of property to a spouse or common-law partner, or a qualifying spousal trust.

  2. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 146.3 ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026. Subsection 146.3(6): the last annuitant of a RRIF is deemed to have received the fund’s fair market value immediately before death; subsection 146.3(6.1): designated benefits.

  3. Canada Revenue Agency · Taxable capital gains on property, investments, and belongings (deceased persons) ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the deemed disposition of investments such as mutual funds at death, the tax-deferred transfer to a surviving spouse (property vested within 36 months) and the election out of that rollover.

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · RRIF, prepare tax returns for someone who died ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the full fair market value of a RRIF being included in the deceased’s income unless the property is paid to and transferred by a surviving spouse, and for successor annuitant elections.

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · RRSP, prepare tax returns for someone who died ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the same treatment of an unmatured RRSP at death and the spouse transfer before the end of the year following death.

  6. Canada Revenue Agency · If you are a designated beneficiary of a TFSA ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for no tax on amounts received up to the TFSA’s fair market value on the date of death, taxable earnings after death, the January 2026 change for survivors’ exempt contributions, and Quebec designation limits.

  7. Canada Revenue Agency · Calculating and reporting your capital gains and losses ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the one-half inclusion rate applied to capital gains in the model.

  8. Government of Ontario · Estate Administration Tax ↗

    Page updated 24 June 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026 for CAD 15 per CAD 1,000 above CAD 50,000 and no tax on estates of CAD 50,000 or less. Used only as an example of a provincial probate fee.
